## Overview

Surveys are often designed for large areas (provinces, regions) but the estimates are needed
for the sub-areas inside them (districts, municipalities). The sub-areas of one area share the
area's characteristics, so their estimates should borrow strength not only from the regression
on auxiliary variables, but also from the other sub-areas of the same area.

The two-fold sub-area level model of Torabi and Rao (2014) does this with two nested random
effects. **fastsae** fits it in two ways:

| Function | Approach | Uncertainty | Area aggregates |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| `eblup_twofold()` | EBLUP, REML or ML | Analytical (Prasad-Rao type) or parametric bootstrap MSE | `df_area`, weighted by `weight` |
| `hb_twofold()` | Hierarchical Bayes with INLA | Posterior SD and credible intervals | `df_area`, weighted by `weight` |

`hb_twofold()` also fits binomial and Poisson responses and a spatial (BYM2, Besag) area effect.

---

## Model

For sub-area $j$ ($j = 1, \dots, N_i$) of area $i$ ($i = 1, \dots, m$), the direct estimator
$y_{ij}$ with known sampling variance $\psi_{ij}$ follows

$$y_{ij} = \theta_{ij} + e_{ij}, \qquad \theta_{ij} = x_{ij}^\top \beta + v_i + u_{ij},$$

with $v_i \sim N(0, \sigma_v^2)$ the area effect, $u_{ij} \sim N(0, \sigma_u^2)$ the sub-area
effect and $e_{ij} \sim N(0, \psi_{ij})$ the sampling error, all independent.

Compared with the Fay-Herriot model, which treats every sub-area as unrelated, the area effect
$v_i$ is estimated from all the sampled sub-areas of area $i$. This matters most for sub-areas
that are not sampled: they get $x_{ij}^\top \hat\beta + \hat v_i$ instead of the synthetic
$x_{ij}^\top \hat\beta$ alone. Only a sub-area of an area without any sample is predicted
synthetically.

The output follows the notation above: `random_effect_var` holds `sigma2_v` (area) and
`sigma2_u` (sub-area), and `df_eblup` (or `df_hb`) holds `random_effect_area` and
`random_effect_subarea`.

---

## Example with simulated data

We simulate 30 areas with 3 to 6 sub-areas each, so that the true sub-area means $\theta_{ij}$
are known. Fifteen sub-areas have no sample (their direct estimate is `NA`), and all the
sub-areas of area `A30` are unsampled.

```{r simulate}
library(fastsae)

set.seed(2024)
m <- 30
dat <- do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_len(m), function(i) {
  ni <- sample(3:6, 1)
  data.frame(
    area = sprintf("A%02d", i),
    subarea = sprintf("A%02d-%d", i, seq_len(ni)),
    x1 = rnorm(ni, mean = 2),
    pop = sample(200:2000, ni)
  )
}))
v <- rnorm(m, sd = 1)
names(v) <- unique(dat$area)
dat$theta <- 10 + 2 * dat$x1 + v[dat$area] + rnorm(nrow(dat), sd = sqrt(0.5))
dat$vardir <- runif(nrow(dat), 0.5, 2)
dat$y <- dat$theta + rnorm(nrow(dat), sd = sqrt(dat$vardir))

# Unsampled sub-areas: 15 at random, plus every sub-area of A30
unsampled <- union(sample(which(dat$area != "A30"), 15), which(dat$area == "A30"))
dat$y[unsampled] <- NA

c(subareas = nrow(dat), sampled = sum(!is.na(dat$y)))
head(dat)
```

Each row is one sub-area. Unsampled sub-areas stay in the data with `y = NA` and their
covariates, so that they are predicted.

### Fitting the EBLUP

```{r fit_eblup}
fit_tf <- eblup_twofold(
  y ~ x1,
  vardir = "vardir",
  domain = "area",
  subarea = "subarea",
  data = dat,
  weight = "pop",
  print_result = FALSE
)

fit_tf$random_effect_var
fit_tf$estcoef
head(fit_tf$df_eblup)
```

The default `mse_type = "analytical"` gives the Prasad-Rao type MSE of the REML fit (for ML it
adds the bias correction). Sub-area `A01-3` is not sampled: it still gets the area effect of
`A01`, while its sub-area effect is 0.

`weight` (here the population of each sub-area) aggregates the sub-area EBLUPs to area means,
$\tilde\theta_i = \sum_j w_{ij}\tilde\theta_{ij} / \sum_j w_{ij}$, in `df_area`. Their MSE
accounts for the errors the sub-areas of an area share (the estimated area effect and
$\hat\beta$), so it is larger than $\sum_j w_{ij}^2\,\mathrm{mse}_{ij}$ would suggest.

```{r area_eblup}
head(fit_tf$df_area)
```

### How much does the area effect help?

Because the data are simulated, we can compare each estimator with the true $\theta_{ij}$.
The Fay-Herriot model, fitted with `eblup_fh()` on the same rows, ignores the areas.

```{r compare_truth}
fit_fh <- eblup_fh(y ~ x1, vardir = "vardir", data = dat, print_result = FALSE)

sampled <- !is.na(dat$y)
in_sampled_area <- !sampled & dat$area != "A30"
emp_mse <- function(est, rows) mean((est[rows] - dat$theta[rows])^2)

data.frame(
  rows = c("sampled sub-areas", "unsampled sub-areas of sampled areas"),
  direct = c(emp_mse(dat$y, sampled), NA),
  fay_herriot = c(
    emp_mse(fit_fh$df_eblup$eblup, sampled),
    emp_mse(fit_fh$df_eblup$eblup, in_sampled_area)
  ),
  two_fold = c(
    emp_mse(fit_tf$df_eblup$eblup, sampled),
    emp_mse(fit_tf$df_eblup$eblup, in_sampled_area)
  )
)
```

Both models improve on the direct estimates of the sampled sub-areas, and in this data set they
are about equally accurate there: a sampled sub-area has its own direct estimate, so the area
effect adds little. The difference is in the unsampled sub-areas of sampled areas. The
Fay-Herriot model can only give them the synthetic estimate, while the two-fold model adds the
estimated area effect and roughly halves the error. This is one simulated data set, not a
simulation study: the gain depends on how large $\sigma_v^2$ is relative to $\sigma_u^2$.

### Bootstrap MSE

The parametric bootstrap refits the model on `B` data sets generated from the fitted model and
predicts with the same estimator as the point estimate. `seed` makes it reproducible without
changing the random number stream of the session.

```{r bootstrap}
fit_boot <- eblup_twofold(
  y ~ x1,
  vardir = "vardir",
  domain = "area",
  subarea = "subarea",
  data = dat,
  mse_type = "bootstrap",
  B = 100,
  seed = 1,
  print_result = FALSE
)

summary(fit_boot$df_eblup$mse / fit_tf$df_eblup$mse)
```

The two MSE estimators agree on average; with `B = 100` single bootstrap values are still
noisy. Use `mse_type = "none"` when only the point estimates are needed.

### Diagnostics and plots

The usual tools of the package work on the result:

```{r diagnostics}
autoplot(fit_tf, type = "comparison")
diagnose(fit_tf)
```

## Hierarchical Bayes with `hb_twofold()`

`hb_twofold()` fits the same model with INLA. It needs the **INLA** package, which is not on
CRAN; see <https://www.r-inla.org/download/>. The chunks below are only run when INLA is
installed.

The argument `weight` (here the population of each sub-area) aggregates the sub-area posteriors
to area estimates, $\hat\theta_i = \sum_j w_{ij} \theta_{ij} / \sum_j w_{ij}$, with their
posterior uncertainty in `df_area`.

```{r fit_hb, eval = has_inla}
fit_hb <- hb_twofold(
  y ~ x1,
  vardir = "vardir",
  domain = "area",
  subarea = "subarea",
  weight = "pop",
  data = dat,
  print_result = FALSE
)

fit_hb$random_effect_var
head(fit_hb$df_hb)
head(fit_hb$df_area)
```

With the default vague priors the posterior means are very close to the EBLUP:

```{r compare_hb, eval = has_inla}
cor(fit_tf$df_eblup$eblup, fit_hb$df_hb$hb)
compare_sae(fit_tf, fit_hb, names = c("EBLUP two-fold", "HB two-fold"))
```

`compare_sae()` reports smaller posterior variances than EBLUP MSEs. The two are not the same
quantity, and here the posterior mean of $\sigma_u^2$ is also smaller than the REML estimate
(both are below the true value 0.5, which is hard to separate from sampling variances of 0.5 to
2). A smaller reported uncertainty is therefore not evidence of a more accurate estimator. With
simulated data, the error against the truth settles it; here the two are practically equal:

```{r truth_hb, eval = has_inla}
c(
  eblup_two_fold = emp_mse(fit_tf$df_eblup$eblup, sampled | in_sampled_area),
  hb_two_fold = emp_mse(fit_hb$df_hb$hb, sampled | in_sampled_area)
)
```

For counts or proportions, use `family = "poisson"` with `exposure` or `family = "binomial"`
with `trials`; with `spatial = "bym2"` and a neighbourhood graph `W` between areas (for
example from `create_weights()`), the area effects are spatially correlated.

### MCMC with `engine = jax_engine()`

The same model can be sampled by MCMC (NumPyro's No-U-Turn sampler on JAX) instead of INLA.
It needs Python with `jax` and `numpyro` (see `?setup_numpyro_env`), so this chunk is not run
here. The result has the same structure, plus the posterior draws in `draws` and the largest
split R-hat in `rhat_max`; the area aggregates in `df_area` come from the MCMC draws.

```{r fit_hb_jax, eval = FALSE}
fit_jax <- hb_twofold(
  y ~ x1,
  vardir = "vardir",
  domain = "area",
  subarea = "subarea",
  weight = "pop",
  data = dat,
  engine = jax_engine(warmup = 1000, samples = 1000, chains = 4),
  print_result = FALSE
)
fit_jax$rhat_max
head(fit_jax$df_area)
```

The priors differ from those of INLA (half-normal standard deviations instead of PC priors), so
the estimates differ slightly; on simulated data with 20 areas the area means of the two engines
correlated above 0.999.

---

## Practical notes

- Give one row per sub-area. The `domain` column identifies the area and is required.
- `vardir` must be finite and positive for every sampled sub-area; unsampled sub-areas can have
  `NA`. Covariates must be complete for all rows, sampled or not.
- At least two areas need sampled sub-areas, otherwise $\sigma_v^2$ cannot be estimated.
- `eblup_twofold()` has `self_benchmark = TRUE` for estimates that add up to a known total (see
  `?eblup_twofold`).

## References

- Torabi, M., & Rao, J. N. K. (2014). On small area estimation under a sub-area level model.
  *Journal of Multivariate Analysis*, 127, 36–55.
- Rao, J. N. K., & Molina, I. (2015). *Small Area Estimation* (2nd ed.). John Wiley & Sons.
- Rue, H., Martino, S., & Chopin, N. (2009). Approximate Bayesian inference for latent Gaussian
  models by using integrated nested Laplace approximations. *Journal of the Royal Statistical
  Society: Series B*, 71(2), 319–392.
